passage: On the local bus to the high school in Sangli, Kalyani noticed the pattern. Last week Vandana had saved her the window seat every day, shared her chikki and chatted non-stop. This week she sat at the back and looked away when Kalyani waved. On Thursday, when Kalyani asked what was wrong, Vandana snapped, "Why do you care?" Kalyani's face stung. At home she almost decided to ignore Vandana for good. Then she remembered how Vandana had gone cold before, right after she said her parents had started fighting at night. Maybe it wasn't about Kalyani at all. On Friday she said, "I'm not okay with being snapped at. But I'm still your friend. Have you told Shinde ma'am about home?" Vandana stared at the fields for a long time. Then she nodded once.

qa.q: What did Vandana share with Kalyani last week?
qa.a: She shared her chikki.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when Vandana snapped "Why do you care?"
qa.a: She felt hurt; her face stung and she almost decided to ignore Vandana for good.

qa.q: What choice did Kalyani make on Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She set a clear limit about being snapped at, stayed a friend and suggested Vandana talk to Shinde ma'am, a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt hearing Kalyani say she was still her friend?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and relieved, and perhaps safer to think about asking an adult for help.

grounding: A teenager sees a friend turn warm then cold, reads it as fear rather than insult, sets a boundary and nudges her toward a trusted adult.

passage: In the Prague school cafeteria on Monday, Oskar sat laughing with Vera, sketching silly portraits of teachers on napkins. By Wednesday he wouldn't answer her messages, and when she sat beside him in chemistry he moved seats. It had happened three times this term. Her first thought was, what did I do? Then she remembered the weeks after his grandmother died, and how he pulled away just when people tried to get close. On Friday she slipped him a note: "I miss you. I won't chase you. But tell me when you need space instead of vanishing. And please talk to someone you trust, maybe Mr Novak or your aunt." Oskar read it twice and put it in his pocket.

qa.q: What did Oskar sketch on napkins?
qa.a: He sketched silly portraits of teachers.

qa.q: What was Vera's first worry when Oskar moved seats?
qa.a: She worried that she had done something wrong.

qa.q: Which parts of Vera's note were wise, and why?
qa.a: She said she missed him, asked him to name his need for space instead of vanishing, and urged him to talk to a trusted adult, which is kind but clear.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel reading the note twice?
qa.a: He may feel cared for without being pressured, which could make it easier for him to reach out.

grounding: A teenager notices a friend who is warm one week and cold the next, sees fear rather than insult, sets a boundary and points him to a trusted adult.

passage: In the hostel, Chaitanya had spent the first week of term glued to Chetan: sharing earphones at prep, saving him a seat in the mess, calling him "brother". Then on Monday, nothing. Chaitanya walked past him in the corridor as if he were a wall and moved to another table at prep. Chetan's first thought was, What did I do? He lay awake replaying every conversation. Then he remembered how Chaitanya had flinched once when a teacher raised his voice, and said he'd changed schools four times. Maybe this wasn't about him. On Thursday Chetan sat down opposite him in the mess. "I'm not going to chase you. I'm here if you want to talk. And Warden-sir listens well, if you'd rather tell a grown-up." Chaitanya didn't answer, but he didn't get up either.

qa.q: How many times had Chaitanya changed schools?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling at first, and how did it change?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, wondering what he did, then began to see Chaitanya's coldness as fear rather than an insult.

qa.q: How did Chetan set a boundary while staying kind?
qa.a: He said he wouldn't chase, stayed available and pointed Chaitanya to the warden as a trusted adult.

qa.q: What might it be like for Chaitanya when Chetan sits down opposite?
qa.a: Chaitanya may feel wary but relieved, since he stays at the table instead of leaving.

grounding: Shows a peer who notices a friend's sudden coldness, reads it as fear, keeps a boundary and suggests a trusted adult.

passage:
Dolma,
I've started this letter four times. Two weeks ago we were laughing over momos after the science fair, and you said I was the only one who got you. Since Monday you've stopped answering, and yesterday you told Pema I was fake. It hurt. I won't pretend it didn't. But I've noticed this happens after we get close, and I wonder if it's something scary rather than something I did. I won't keep messaging every day; I'll be at the library bench at lunch on Fridays. And if things feel too big, Mrs Lepcha, the counsellor, is kind. I went to her in Class 8. You don't have to tell me anything.
Harish

qa.q: Where will Harish be on Fridays?
qa.a: At the library bench at lunch.

qa.q: What is Harish feeling about Dolma's sudden coldness?
qa.a: Harish feels hurt but is trying to understand it as fear rather than a personal insult.

qa.q: What makes Harish's letter a wise response?
qa.a: It names the hurt, sets a clear limit on messaging, stays available and points to a trusted counsellor.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Dolma may feel understood and less cornered, since the letter asks for nothing and leaves a door open.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who notices warm-then-cold shifts, reads them as fear, sets a boundary and suggests a trusted adult.

passage: So you know Santosh, from my tuition? Last month we were inseparable, I'm not exaggerating: walking home together, sharing notes, laughing about everything. Then one Tuesday he looked through me like I was a stranger. My first reaction was, fine, be like that. I'm Bidisha, and I don't beg. But I watched him that week. He was jumpy, snapping at everyone, not just me. I remembered him saying his older brother had moved abroad last year and he hated talking about it. So instead of getting angry, I told him, "I'm not going anywhere, but I won't be treated like dirt either." And then: "You should talk to Ma'am at tuition, or the school counsellor." He shrugged. The next day I saw him walk into the counsellor's room.

qa.q: What did Bidisha see Santosh do the next day?
qa.a: Walk into the counsellor's room.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Santosh first looked through her?
qa.a: Bidisha felt hurt, a bit proud and angry, thinking "fine, be like that", before seeing it differently.

qa.q: How did Bidisha balance kindness and limits?
qa.a: Bidisha stayed available, refused to be treated badly and encouraged Santosh to talk to a trusted adult.

qa.q: Why might Santosh have gone cold after being close?
qa.a: He may be scared of losing people after his brother moved abroad, so closeness feels risky.

grounding: Shows a peer who sees a friend turn cold, reads it as fear, keeps a clear boundary and encourages a trusted adult.

passage:
I'm Mohit, and Lakshmi has been in my tuition batch since Class 8.
Some weeks she saves me a seat, shares her notes and texts me every night. Then, out of nowhere, she won't look at me. Last Monday I said hi and she walked straight past. I was hurt, honestly. I thought I'd done something.
I don't know what goes on inside her. But on Thursday she said, "Everyone leaves eventually, so what's the point?" and her voice cracked.
I didn't get angry. I said, "I'm not going anywhere. But I can't keep guessing, so if you're upset with me, tell me." Then I asked if she'd talk to Mrs Pillai, our tuition teacher, who she trusts.
She said maybe. After class, I walked with her to Mrs Pillai's desk. Mrs Pillai asked me to wait outside and talked with her for a long time.

qa.q: Who did Mohit suggest Lakshmi talk to?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai, their tuition teacher, who she trusts.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when Lakshmi walked past without looking?
qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and unsure, wondering if Mohit had done something wrong.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that was both kind and clear?
qa.a: Mohit reassured Lakshmi without anger, set a boundary about not guessing, and walked her to a trusted adult.

qa.q: What might be going on for Lakshmi when she turns cold?
qa.a: Her words "Everyone leaves eventually" suggest she may be afraid of being left, so pulling away first might feel safer, though Mohit can't know for sure.

grounding: Shows a friend who sees warm-then-cold swings as possible fear rather than insult, sets a clear boundary and brings in a trusted adult.
